metadata.description: The official Ryu plugin marketplace — declarative, UI-less tools.

plugins.name: activity
plugins.tagline: Everything happening on this node, newest first
plugins.description: The unified activity feed: everything happening on this node — monitor alerts, finished tasks, runs, approvals, meetings, and notes — newest first, grouped by day.

plugins.name: advisor
plugins.tagline: A stronger second model reviews your answers
plugins.description: Consult a stronger reviewer model for a second opinion — as an auto-review turn hook (toggle / `/advisor`) and as the model-callable `advisor__consult` tool, a declarative HTTP tool routed through Core's `/api/advisor/consult` bridge.

plugins.name: agent-status
plugins.tagline: See which agents are working, stuck, or done
plugins.description: Splits your agent runs across three sidebar sections — Working, Needs input and Done — each row showing the project it belongs to.

plugins.name: agentbrowser
plugins.tagline: A second real browser for the browser.control layer
plugins.description: Browser automation via the `agent-browser` CLI's MCP server (https://agent-browser.dev). Provides the swappable `browser.control` layer, so selecting it re-points the stable `browser__*` tools at agent-browser without changing what agents call. Launched via `npx agent-browser mcp`; needs Node on PATH.

plugins.name: approvals
plugins.tagline: Nothing happens until you say yes
plugins.description: Approval inbox: a human-in-the-loop queue where agent-proposed actions, edits, and fixes wait for your accept or reject before they take effect.

plugins.name: brave
plugins.tagline: Search an index nobody else syndicates
plugins.description: Independent web search via the Brave Search API (https://brave.com/search/api/), exposed as one declarative HTTP tool. Provides the swappable `web.search` layer, so selecting it in the layer picker re-points the stable `web__search` tool at Brave's own crawled index without changing what agents call. Brave is search-only: it deliberately declares neither `web.extract` nor `web.crawl`. Requires a BYOK Brave Search API key.

plugins.name: browser
plugins.tagline: Real-Chromium browser control for agents
plugins.description: A real-Chromium browser (Electron) Ryu runs as a local sidecar and exposes as the grant-gated `browser.control` capability: list/open/navigate tabs, screenshot, read titles, take an accessibility snapshot with stable element refs, and drive the page with synthetic click/type/scroll input. Core spawns the sidecar lazily and idle-stops it; the desktop Browser panel drives it through the ext-proxy.

plugins.name: bytebot
plugins.tagline: Swap computer control onto a Bytebot desktop
plugins.description: Drives a Bytebot desktop (https://github.com/bytebot-ai/bytebot) through `bytebotd`, its local HTTP daemon, as the SECOND provider of the swappable `computer.control` layer — the first thing that makes that layer actually swappable rather than merely marked selectable. READ THIS BEFORE SELECTING IT: bytebotd drives the desktop IT runs on, which in the shipped Bytebot product is a containerized Linux desktop, NOT the machine running Ryu. Selecting it re-points `computer__capture` / `computer__click` / `computer__type` / `computer__key` / `computer__scroll` away from your own screen (`ghost`, the declared default) and onto that desktop — the same remote-target relationship `browser.control` already has between the local Chromium sidecar and a hosted browser. It serves FIVE of the six canonical verbs: `computer__focus_app` is deliberately NOT bound, because bytebotd's `application` action takes a closed seven-value enum (firefox, 1password, thunderbird, vscode, terminal, desktop, directory) while the canonical verb takes a free-form app name, so any other name would be a schema-legal call that 400s. The app switch is still reachable natively as `bytebot__application`, whose own schema carries that enum so an illegal call cannot be composed. Requires no API key — bytebotd ships with no authentication at all, which is also why this plugin only ever addresses it over loopback. SECURITY, read before enabling: bytebotd ships with NO authentication — no auth middleware, permissive CORS — and this plugin reaches it at the fixed loopback port 9990. Its egress grant is `tool:http-egress:127.0.0.1`, which is HOST-scoped, not port-scoped: approving it grants reach to any service on loopback, not just bytebotd. Only enable this on a machine where you accept that an unauthenticated desktop-control daemon is running and reachable. TARGET: bytebotd drives the desktop IT runs on — in the shipped Bytebot product that is a containerized Linux desktop, NOT the machine running Ryu — so selecting this instead of `ghost` does not give you another way to drive your own computer.

plugins.name: calendar
plugins.tagline: Every scheduled run on one calendar
plugins.description: The scheduled-runs calendar: every agent and workflow scheduled job projected onto Month, Week, Day, and Agenda views — past runs from history, upcoming runs from cron/interval — with a New automation dialog that schedules an agent.

plugins.name: canvas
plugins.tagline: Wire up media and agent nodes on one board
plugins.description: A node board for generative media: wire up image, video, chat, text-to-speech, speech-to-text, upload, and note nodes, then run the graph through Ryu's media and agent bridges. Each board persists as a Space document, so it stays editable, shareable, and searchable.

plugins.name: chat-title
plugins.tagline: Names your chats for you, automatically
plugins.description: Auto-renames a chat after every N completed assistant turns (default 5) using a side model, and keeps a Core-side history of the names it chose so you can see how a conversation drifted. Enablement, frequency, and the model to use are all settings.

plugins.name: clips
plugins.tagline: Capture and browse screen clips
plugins.description: Clips: capture and browse screen/timeline clips. A Core→Shadow proxy that depends on the Shadow capture app for its recordings. Runs the out-of-process ryu-clips sidecar; Core proxies /api/clips/* to it. The Shadow record/browse surface is fully served out-of-process (the sidecar reads RYU_SHADOW_URL itself); URL/yt-dlp ingest and auto-file into the Clips Space require Core's kernel machinery and degrade cleanly in the standalone sidecar.

plugins.name: dashboards
plugins.tagline: Live widget boards over your node
plugins.description: Dashboards: composable widget boards that assemble live views over monitors, meetings, quests, and other Core surfaces via soft HTTP loopback. Declares the out-of-process ryu-dashboards sidecar (kind:local) that owns the store + refresh loop + /api/dashboards/* surface, served to the desktop through the generic ext-proxy public_mount. Started eagerly (not lazy) so the kernel hardware device-dashboard renderer + nudge loop can reach it at boot / on a device poll before any desktop has opened Home. The dashboard_builder MCP runnable + the hardware render seam reach it over loopback via dashboards_client.

plugins.name: dictation
plugins.tagline: Speak anywhere, type anywhere
plugins.description: System-wide dictation and agent-ask via the Island companion: speak anywhere to type a transcript, or ask an agent and paste the answer into the focused app.

plugins.name: docling
plugins.tagline: Layout-aware parsing, tables that survive chunking
plugins.description: Document parsing via IBM's MIT-licensed Docling — the highest-fidelity `document.parse` backend. Where a text extractor hands a model a stream of characters, Docling runs real layout analysis: a page-segmentation model finds the reading order, a table-structure model rebuilds merged cells and spanning headers, and the result is exported as markdown whose headings, lists and tables mirror the document's actual structure. That is what makes a multi-column paper or a financial statement survive chunking instead of interleaving into nonsense. The cost is weight: the first parse downloads its models (hundreds of MB) and can take minutes, and every parse after that is CPU-bound inference rather than a string copy. Everything runs locally — Docling explicitly supports air-gapped operation once the models are cached — and no document ever leaves the node. Parses run as jobs: submit returns 202 + a job_id, the caller polls.

plugins.name: double-check
plugins.tagline: A second model reviews every answer
plugins.description: Sends every answer to a second model for review before you act on it, so mistakes get caught by a fresh set of eyes. Off until you flip the Double-check toggle in the composer; the reviewer model is configurable in settings.

plugins.name: exa
plugins.tagline: Neural web search for agents
plugins.description: Neural and keyword web search via the Exa API (https://exa.ai), exposed as two declarative HTTP tools: search and find-similar. Requires a BYOK Exa API key.

plugins.name: finetune
plugins.tagline: Train a model on your own data, on your own GPU
plugins.description: A LoRA/QLoRA training studio: launch fine-tune jobs on this node's GPU or a remote Ryu Cloud GPU node, track them durably, merge the trained adapter to GGUF, and register the result as a swappable local model.

plugins.name: firecrawl
plugins.tagline: Search and scrape the web for agents
plugins.description: Web search and page scraping via the Firecrawl v2 API (https://firecrawl.dev), exposed as two declarative HTTP tools. Provides the swappable `web.search` and `web.extract` layers, so selecting it in the layer picker re-points the stable `web__search` / `web__extract` tools at Firecrawl without changing what agents call. Requires a BYOK Firecrawl API key.

plugins.name: firewall
plugins.tagline: Turn on the Gateway's prompt-injection and PII screen
plugins.description: An on/off switch over the Gateway's built-in firewall, which screens model traffic for prompt injection and PII. Enabling this plugin forces `firewall.enabled` on at the next Gateway restart; the pattern set and policy mode stay owned by the Gateway config (GET/PUT /v1/config), not by this plugin.

plugins.name: ghost
plugins.tagline: Let agents see and drive your desktop
plugins.description: Desktop automation: 29 screen perception and input control tools. Windows-first.

plugins.name: goal
plugins.tagline: Keep working until a judge model says it's done
plugins.description: Give the agent a goal with `/goal` and it keeps working until a judge model agrees the goal is actually met, re-prompting itself after every turn instead of stopping and waiting for you. `/goal clear` stops the loop; the judge model is configurable.

plugins.name: headroom
plugins.tagline: Compress noisy context down to a fraction of its tokens
plugins.description: Context compression (chopratejas/headroom): compress tool outputs, logs, files, and RAG chunks. 60-95% fewer tokens, reversible retrieval. Requires headroom-ai[mcp].

plugins.name: healing
plugins.tagline: Failed runs diagnose and fix themselves — with your approval
plugins.description: Self-healing: failed runs are diagnosed by a Gateway side-model and proposed fixes are delivered to the approvals inbox for human review before they apply.

plugins.name: honcho
plugins.tagline: A standing synthesis of the user, not a list of facts
plugins.description: Give the swappable `memory` layer a provider that MODELS the user instead of only storing rows, via Honcho (https://honcho.dev) — the Plastic Labs identity layer Hermes uses for exactly this. Honcho watches the messages you hand it and derives a per-peer REPRESENTATION; its Dialectic endpoint (`POST /v3/workspaces/{workspace_id}/peers/{peer_id}/chat`) then answers a natural-language question about that peer with its own synthesis. That is what the canonical `memory__context` verb has always promised and no shipped provider served, so this is the first plugin to make the kernel's `context` bridge (`memory.provider-context`) do anything at all. Honcho here serves TWO verbs: `memory__context` (the Dialectic synthesis) and `memory__search` (`POST .../peers/{peer_id}/search`, documented as "Search a Peer's messages" — conversation text, not the conclusions Honcho derives from it, which matters because the `prefetch` bridge is on by default and will start injecting message excerpts each turn). It also binds the two WRITE verbs, `memory__sync` and `memory__store`, through an adapter. Honcho's only documented write is `POST /v3/workspaces/{workspace_id}/sessions/{session_id}/messages`, whose `messages[]` items each require a `peer_id` — a NESTED position the declarative `arg_template` cannot reach, because a template substitutes only from CALLER arguments and never sees a resolved `pref:`. That is why both verbs went unbound and why `memory.mirror-builtin` (default ON) was inert. An adapter receives those `pref:` values already resolved, so the per-install peer lands inside `messages[]` without hardcoding one bucket for every install. The session and both peers are caller-named and created on first write, so nothing has to be set up by hand; Ryu's own replies are written as a SEPARATE peer, since attributing an assistant turn to your peer would poison the representation Honcho derives about you. `memory__forget` stays unbound: Honcho documents no message-delete endpoint, which no adapter can invent. The built-in store's own `memorystore__save` tool and this node's per-turn memory write are kernel and untouched. Every call is scoped to one workspace and one peer, both set per install in the settings tab — a hardcoded pair would put every install in one shared bucket. Requires a BYOK Honcho API key.

plugins.name: hook-observers
plugins.tagline: Reference plugin: one observer per hook event
plugins.description: A worked reference for the turn-hook events Ryu can fire: five observer hooks watching subagent-stop, session-end, notification, workflow-run-failed, and a third-party app event (`com.ryu.meetings#meeting.ended`), each returning a harmless note. Nothing in Core knows this plugin exists — copy the directory as the starting point for your own event-driven plugin.

plugins.name: hook-session-context
plugins.tagline: Tell the agent what today's date is
plugins.description: Injects the current date and time at the start of every session, so the agent stops guessing what "today" means and can reason about recency and deadlines. Also the smallest working turn hook in the catalog, which makes it a good template to copy.

plugins.name: learning
plugins.tagline: Turn your chats into reusable skills
plugins.description: Learning loop: turn chats and runs into reusable skills, gated by the approval Inbox, with an experience log of what was learned.

plugins.name: mail
plugins.tagline: Email inboxes for your agents
plugins.description: Agent Inboxes — email as a service for agents. Runs the out-of-process ryu-mail sidecar; Core proxies /api/mail/* to it. Its sandboxed companion is a per-node mail client (list inboxes, read messages, compose/send, create an inbox) driving /api/mail/* via the mail:crud bridge capability.

plugins.name: markitdown
plugins.tagline: Pure-pip document parsing, no native toolchain
plugins.description: Document parsing via Microsoft's MIT-licensed MarkItDown library — the default `document.parse` backend, and the one that works on a machine where the user installed nothing on purpose. `pip install 'markitdown[all]'` is a pure-Python install of a few tens of megabytes: no ONNX runtime, no layout-detection model download, no GPU, and no `brew`/`apt` packages to chase. It covers the formats people actually attach — PDF, DOCX, PPTX, XLSX/XLS, HTML, CSV, JSON, XML, EPUB, Outlook .msg, Jupyter notebooks, and ZIP archives expanded member-by-member — and it emits markdown natively rather than a flat text dump, so headings stay headings and spreadsheet tables stay tables. The tradeoffs are honest ones: no OCR (a scanned PDF comes back empty and the job says so), no legacy binary `.doc`/`.ppt`, and no element-level structure for a consumer that wants to chunk on document structure. Parses run as jobs: submit returns 202 + a job_id, the caller polls.

plugins.name: meetings
plugins.tagline: Record, transcribe, and write up your meetings
plugins.description: Meeting notes: record → live transcript → AI notes, auto-saved into the Meetings Space so they stay editable and RAG-searchable.

plugins.name: mem0
plugins.tagline: Recall and record in an existing Mem0 project inside Ryu
plugins.description: Read and write a hosted Mem0 memory project (https://mem0.ai) through the Mem0 Platform REST API, exposed as three declarative HTTP tools. The SECOND provider of the swappable `memory` layer — the built-in store stays the default and keeps running alongside it — so selecting Mem0 re-points the stable `memory__search` / `memory__store` / `memory__sync` / `memory__forget` tools at your Mem0 project without changing what agents call, and turns on the kernel bridges that fold Mem0 into every turn's recall and echo this node's writes out to it. The one canonical verb Mem0 does NOT serve is `memory__context`: Mem0 publishes no standing-summary endpoint, and forcing the verb onto its get-all would dump raw facts at system rank under a label promising a synthesis. The two WRITE verbs both post to `POST /v3/memories/add/`, which is ASYNCHRONOUS — it answers `{message, status: "PENDING", event_id}` and never a fact id — so `memory__store` returns an accepted-for-processing envelope, not the id of the fact it created, and nothing may chain `memory__forget` onto its result. That is fine for the way both verbs are used: the kernel `mirror` and `sync` bridges are fire-and-forget and never read the response. The two verbs differ in ONE documented field: `store` sends `infer: false` because the caller has already decided the fact and Mem0 should keep the text as-is, while `sync` hands over a raw turn with Mem0's default inference on and lets Mem0 mine it. Note the entity id lives in two different places in Mem0's own API — nested inside `filters` for search, top-level for add — and both are pinned from the same `mem0.user-id` preference. Requires a BYOK Mem0 API key.

plugins.name: mineru
plugins.tagline: Scientific and scanned PDFs, formulas to LaTeX
plugins.description: Document parsing via MinerU (opendatalab) — the highest-fidelity `document.parse` backend, and the heaviest. Built for scientific and scanned PDFs: it runs layout detection to reconstruct true reading order across multi-column pages, converts formulas to LaTeX, converts tables to HTML, and OCRs scanned pages, so a physics paper comes back as markdown a model can actually follow instead of two columns interleaved line by line. The cost is real: MinerU wants Python 3.10-3.13, 16 GB of RAM (32 GB recommended), about 20 GB of disk for its model set, and a 4 GB-VRAM GPU for the pipeline backend (8 GB for the VLM backends) to be quick — a CPU-only host works through the `pipeline` backend but parses take minutes. Models download on first use. MinerU ships as a CLI, so each parse is a supervised subprocess with a hard wall-clock kill: a timed-out or cancelled parse takes its whole process group with it rather than leaving a multi-gigabyte orphan. Parses run as jobs: submit returns 202 + a job_id, the caller polls.

plugins.name: monitors
plugins.tagline: Watch a page and get told when it changes
plugins.description: Website monitors: price, stock, keyword, content, and uptime watches with cross-device notification fan-out.

plugins.name: output-styles
plugins.tagline: Change how the agent talks, not what it knows
plugins.description: The six built-in output styles — ELI5, I have ADHD, Explanatory, Learning, Proactive and Plain text. A style is appended to (or replaces) the agent's base instructions for the turn, so it changes how the agent talks — role, tone, default response shape — and never what it knows, which tools it has, or which model runs. Pick one in the composer; browse them in the Store's Output Styles tab.

plugins.name: parallel
plugins.tagline: Objective-driven web search built for agent loops
plugins.description: Web search and content extraction via Parallel (https://parallel.ai), exposed as three declarative HTTP tools. Provides the swappable `web.search` and `web.extract` layers, so selecting it in the layer picker re-points the stable `web__search` / `web__extract` tools at Parallel without changing what agents call. Search works with NO key through Parallel's public Search MCP endpoint; a BYOK Parallel API key unlocks the higher-limit REST API and extraction.

plugins.name: pi-shell
plugins.tagline: Run long commands without holding the turn open
plugins.description: Adds bash_background / bash_output / bash_kill to the managed Pi agent, so a long-running command does not hold the turn open.

plugins.name: pi-subagent
plugins.tagline: Let the agent delegate work to child agents
plugins.description: Adds the Task tool to the managed Pi agent, so it can delegate a bounded, context-isolated job to a child agent.

plugins.name: plan-continue
plugins.tagline: Stop typing "continue" during plan mode
plugins.description: While plan mode is on and the plan has not been accepted, this injects a follow-up turn after each completed turn asking the agent to carry on planning — so a plan never stalls waiting for you to type "continue".

plugins.name: predict
plugins.tagline: Ghost-text autocomplete in every text field
plugins.description: Inline ghost-text autocomplete in any text field on your machine, accepted with Tab. A small companion reads the caret context and asks Core for a completion, and every prediction is routed through the Gateway — so no model id, Gateway URL, or policy ever lives in the companion process. Windows-first.

plugins.name: proof
plugins.tagline: Keep going until a verifier proves it's done
plugins.description: The stricter sibling of `/goal`: an independent verifier agent has to prove with tool-gathered evidence that the goal is actually done, rather than judging the transcript alone. The loop runs until that proof lands; `/proof clear` stops it and the verifier model is configurable.

plugins.name: pxpipe
plugins.tagline: Pay vision-token prices for the boring half of every prompt
plugins.description: Token-saving loopback proxy (https://github.com/teamchong/pxpipe): it renders the bulky, static parts of a request — the system prompt, the tool-schema block, large tool results and older history — into PNG pages and sends them as image blocks, which vision models price by pixel area rather than by character. Dense text lands at roughly 3.1 characters per image-token against 1 per text-token, so the same budget carries ~4.7x more context; recent turns and sparse content stay as text. This plugin owns the process lifecycle (spawn, health, restart) and mounts pxpipe's dashboard behind Core auth. It is a TRANSPARENT proxy and holds no credential of its own: it forwards whatever key its caller sends, so point a custom provider at http://127.0.0.1:47821 with your own API key (see README). Runs `npx -y pxpipe-proxy@0.11.1`; needs Node on PATH and fetches the package on first start.

plugins.name: quests
plugins.tagline: Your todos, found for you
plugins.description: Quests: auto-detecting todos surfaced from your chats and activity, tracked as a lightweight quest board with progress and completion.

plugins.name: recipes
plugins.tagline: Record a UI sequence once, replay it forever
plugins.description: Desktop-automation recipes: record → save → replay UI action sequences. Backed by Ghost's RecipeStore, so it declares Ghost as a dependency and the graph refuses to disable Ghost out from under it.

plugins.name: research
plugins.tagline: Multi-step web research with cited sources
plugins.description: Deep research: multi-step web research runs backed by the autoresearch sidecar, with sources, findings, and RAG-searchable reports. Declares the out-of-process ryu-research sidecar (a thin Rust proxy that forwards /api/research/* to the Python autoresearch engine on :8087); Core reaches it via the generic ext-proxy loader.

plugins.name: rtk
plugins.tagline: Token-compress noisy dev-command output for agents
plugins.description: Run a dev command through RTK (Rust Token Killer) and get a token-compressed version of its output (60-90% fewer tokens), exposed as a declarative `command` tool that shells out to the locally-installed `rtk` binary. BYO — no API key.

plugins.name: sample
plugins.tagline: Reference plugin: one of every runnable kind
plugins.description: The reference plugin: a minimal example that declares one of each runnable kind — an agent, a workflow, a tool, and a skill — plus a companion window. It does nothing useful on purpose, and ships hidden. Copy this directory as the starting point for your own plugin.

plugins.name: sample-widget
plugins.tagline: Reference plugin: an inline chat widget
plugins.description: Reference third-party MCP widget plugin. A tiny local Node MCP server (server.mjs) exposes one render tool (sample_widget__render) that returns structured data AND serves a self-contained skybridge HTML resource (ui://widget/sample.html). contributes.widgets binds the tool to that resource; the widget:render grant + this manifest are the consent gate that lets Core promote the tool's result into an inline chat widget. Copy this directory as the starting point for your own widget plugin.

plugins.name: scrapling
plugins.tagline: Anti-bot page extraction, no API key
plugins.description: Adaptive web-page extraction via the Scrapling MCP server (https://scrapling.readthedocs.io), a BYO local install. Provides the swappable `web.extract` layer as a THIRD provider alongside the local `spider` CLI and the hosted BYOK services, so selecting it re-points the stable `web__extract` tool at a fetcher that impersonates a real browser TLS fingerprint. No API key. Requires `pip install "scrapling[ai]"` and the `scrapling` binary on PATH; until then the MCP server does not start and the layer falls back to whichever other provider you select. Deliberately provides NO `web.crawl`: neither the MCP server nor the CLI follows links — only Scrapling's Python `Spider` class crawls, and it is not reachable over MCP.

plugins.name: security-guidance
plugins.tagline: Catch vulnerabilities before you ship them
plugins.description: Scans each answer for security vulnerabilities and has a second model review the code before you ship it. Off until you flip the Security review toggle in the composer, or run `/security` for a one-off review of the last answer; the reviewer model is configurable.

plugins.name: serper
plugins.tagline: Google's real results, as JSON, in a second
plugins.description: Google's own search results as JSON via the Serper API (https://serper.dev), plus single-page scraping, exposed as two declarative HTTP tools. Provides the swappable `web.search` and `web.extract` layers, so selecting it in the layer picker re-points the stable `web__search` / `web__extract` tools at Serper without changing what agents call. Serper is a paid, credit-metered API with a free allowance; requires a BYOK Serper API key.

plugins.name: shadow
plugins.tagline: Recall what you have seen and done
plugins.description: Search everything Shadow has captured (screen text, audio transcripts, input) and summarize recent activity. Exposed as declarative HTTP tools that reach the device-local Shadow sidecar through Core's authenticated `/api/shadow/*` proxy (which injects Shadow's bearer token).

plugins.name: simulator
plugins.tagline: iOS Simulator & Android Emulator control for agents
plugins.description: Drive iOS Simulators (macOS + Xcode) and Android Emulators from a workspace tab. Ryu runs the device-control toolchain (`simctl`, `adb`) as a local sidecar and exposes the grant-gated `simulator.control` capability: list/boot devices, install & launch apps, open deep links, screenshot, and (Android) tap/swipe/type. The desktop Simulator panel shows whichever platform the connected node supports.

plugins.name: skill-editor
plugins.tagline: Write and version your own agent skills
plugins.description: Author a user-owned Agent Skill (SKILL.md): front-matter fields (name / description / allowed tools / always-on), a markdown body editor, debounced autosave, and server-backed undoable version history.

plugins.name: spider
plugins.tagline: Crawl and extract web pages for agents
plugins.description: High-performance web crawling and content extraction via the Spider CLI (https://spider.cloud), exposed as a declarative `command` tool that shells out to the locally-installed `spider` binary. No API key.

plugins.name: spidercloud
plugins.tagline: Hosted site crawling, no local binary
plugins.description: Hosted multi-page web crawling via the Spider Cloud API (https://spider.cloud), exposed as one declarative HTTP tool. Provides the swappable `web.crawl` layer as a SECOND provider alongside the local `spider` CLI, so selecting it re-points the stable `web__crawl` tool at a hosted crawler that needs no local binary. The crawl is synchronous — `run_in_background` defaults to false and one request returns every fetched page's content, so there is no job id to poll. The canonical `depth` argument is deliberately DROPPED: Spider Cloud documents `depth: 0` as "no limit will be applied", the exact inverse of the canonical contract's "0 = the start page only". Requires a BYOK Spider Cloud API key.

plugins.name: tavily
plugins.tagline: Agent-tuned web search and extraction
plugins.description: Search-and-extract for agents via the Tavily API (https://tavily.com), exposed as two declarative HTTP tools. Provides the swappable `web.search` and `web.extract` layers, so selecting it in the layer picker re-points the stable `web__search` / `web__extract` tools at Tavily without changing what agents call. Requires a BYOK Tavily API key.

plugins.name: teams
plugins.tagline: Address a group of agents as one
plugins.description: Teams: named groups of agents you can address as one. Governance shell over the in-crate teams store (agent-id membership only); no documents, no external dependencies. Runs the out-of-process ryu-teams sidecar; Core proxies /api/teams/* to it.

plugins.name: timeline
plugins.tagline: Scrub back through everything your screen did
plugins.description: The activity replay timeline: a CapCut-style scrubber over Shadow's captured screen/input/window/audio lanes with a keyframe preview, a Dayflow work journal, and jump-to-moment focus.

plugins.name: tool-firewall
plugins.tagline: Reference plugin: block destructive tool calls
plugins.description: A worked reference for pre- and post-tool hooks: the pre hook denies any tool call whose input matches a destructive pattern (`rm -rf`, `DROP TABLE`, `mkfs`), and the post hook notes what each tool returned. The pattern set is deliberately tiny — copy this directory as the starting point for your own tool policy.

plugins.name: unstructured
plugins.tagline: Sixty formats, element-typed output
plugins.description: Document parsing via the Apache-2.0 Unstructured library — the broadest-coverage `document.parse` backend, reading roughly sixty formats (PDF, the whole Office family including the legacy binary .doc/.ppt/.xls, email, EPUB, HTML, spreadsheets, and OCR over scanned images). Its distinguishing output is element-level: every fragment comes back typed (Title, NarrativeText, ListItem, Table, CodeSnippet, PageBreak), so the sidecar can emit markdown that preserves document structure instead of a flat text dump — headings stay headings and tables stay tables through chunking. The cost is install weight: `unstructured[all-docs]` is a 1-2 GB Python install, and the native tools it shells out to (poppler, tesseract, libreoffice, pandoc) are NOT pip-installable and must be present on the host. The sidecar detects each missing tool and reports it by name through the job's `error`/`missing_dependencies` fields rather than failing as an empty document. Parses run as jobs: submit returns 202 + a job_id, the caller polls.

plugins.name: voice
